message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
## What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the tile next to it**, so you get a little ridge you can feel with your foot or see when light hits it from the side.

It's more likely with long tiles like yours, because large porcelain tiles are often very slightly bowed in the middle. Two things help:
- **Use a ⅓ offset, not ½,** if you lay them in a brick pattern. Lining the bowed middle of one tile up against the edge of the next makes the ridges worse.
- **Use a tile levelling clip system:** cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets.

## Grout colour

For pale grey porcelain, choose **a mid grey a shade or two darker than the tile**. It hides dirt far better than white or very light grout, and it still looks clean. Two extras that help:
- a stain-resistant or "easy clean" grout, or
- a grout sealer applied after it cures.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first.** Tiling the whole floor means the toilet sits on a finished surface, you avoid fiddly cuts around its base, and you won't find an untiled gap if you change the toilet later.

## How many boxes

| | |
|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²** |
| One tile | 0.3 × 0.6 = **0.18 m²** |
| Tiles without waste | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24 tiles** |
| With 10% extra | 26.4, so **27 tiles** |
| Per box | 8 tiles (1.44 m²) |

**Buy 4 boxes (32 tiles).** Three boxes (24 tiles) would be just enough with no allowance for any cuts or breakages.

The 5 or so spares are useful. Keep a couple for repairs later, since tiles from a different batch can vary in shade.

Two layout notes:
- On paper, 4 tiles fit exactly along the 2.4 m wall and 6 tiles along the 1.8 m wall. In reality, grout joints, uneven walls and the toilet waste pipe mean you'll still have cuts.
- A ⅓ offset brick pattern also creates more cuts at the edges.

## Note for the neighbours

> Hi! Just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise for a few hours from around [10am]. Thanks so much for your patience with the skip too. It'll be gone soon, I promise! If anything's a problem, just knock. [Name], no. [house number]

## Three beginner tips

1. **Prepare the floor properly.** It needs to be solid, clean and flat. Long tiles show every dip, so check with a long straight edge and fix low spots with self-levelling compound first. On a wooden floor, add tile backer board or ply, and prime as the adhesive instructions say.
2. **Dry-lay before you stick anything down.** Arrange tiles on the floor without adhesive to plan where the cuts go. Avoid thin slivers at doorways or the most visible edges. Start from the doorway's line of sight, and work back toward the door so you don't tile yourself into a corner.
3. **Work in small sections and get full coverage.** Mix small batches of adhesive, spread it with the right notched trowel, and **back-butter** each tile (spread a thin layer on the back too). Press and slide the tile into place, then lift the first one to check the back is fully covered. Use levelling clips, check with a spirit level often, and stay off the floor until the adhesive has fully cured.

The videos make it look easy because they're edited. If you go slowly and check your work as you go, it's very doable for a first attempt. Good luck!
